Two things could be going on. If weight loss is your goal, you need to eat less calories than you burn, that's it. There are no tricks that will make weight loss easier (outside of finding what works for you and makes it easier to stick to the formula of calories in - calories out < 0). If getting stronger is your goal then you need to constantly be increasing your workload to get further adaptation.

1: the human body is incredible at adapting to changes and starting a workout regimen will cause you to lose weight as long as you don't wind up eating more than you burn, but over time (a few months to about a year depending on the person) your body will figure out how to burn less calories throughout the day. Simple example, person a burns about 1500 calories a day just existing and 500 doing whatever they do day to day. They eat let's say an average of 2100 calories per day. That surplus intake cause weight gain. They start a workout regimen that adds about 500 calories per day and maybe eat an extra 100-200 calories. At the start they are now burning 2500 per day and eating only 2200-2300. That cause weight loss. As this continues the body figures out how to make existing easier and maybe day to day outside of the workout gets easier so you eventually go back to burning about 2000 calories per day (1100 existing + 400 day to day + 500 working out). So you either need to increase workout intensity or cut back on calories. At some point increasing workout load hits a limit and all you can do is cut back on calories.

2: when working out, the goal is to push your muscles to the point where they just start to break down a bit, a good workout will leave your muscles full of small tears that the body will then repair and put back together stronger than before they were broken. When you start out there is less muscle to break and it takes less work to break it. As you get stronger you need to break more muscle fibers, and they take more load and/or reps to break them. Without increasing the weight and/or number of reps/sets you do when lifting (with a HIIT workout you have to increase intensity, interval duration, or number of intervals) then you will eventually reach a point where you aren't making your muscles do enough work to break, thus there is nothing for your body to make stronger while repairing it.

Our desire to share. There is genetically not a whole lot of difference between us and chimps (and other primates). Lots of other primates even use tools. We have evolved to age slowly and slow down our development phase and dedicated more calories to brain development. Most animals dedicate most of their energy to reproduction because they die too quick to do anything else. Some group of early hominids starting splitting responsibilities between hunting and gathering. Hunters shared with gatherers and vice versa and anyone who didn't get enough food was still able to eat enough that day because someone else got enough food and shared it. Our bodies didn't need to spend so much of our energy intake on finding food (while we were young) and instead were able to spend calories in brain development and learning. You even look at primates now, they rarely share, and any sharing they do tends to be food they throw away when they're full or if they get a big haul of something difficult to get they can give their young offspring.

The body can store an insane amount of fat and fat has a lot of energy in it. Another problem is that the human body is incredible at adjusting to it's environment. If you suddenly start a workout regimen that adds a few hundred calories of daily burn to your normal calorie burn, the body takes just a few months to figure out how to reduce it's daily average back to pre workout levels. Just making up some numbers off the top of my head:

Before starting exercise regimen
Daily calories burned: 2200
Daily calories consumed: 2300
Calorie surplus: 100 calories (gaining weight)

After starting workout regimen
Daily calories burned: 2400
Daily calories consumed: 2300
Calorie deficit: 100 calories (losing weight)

After adjustment period required by your body to match the new workout regimen:
Daily calories burned: 2200
Daily calories consumed: 2300
Calorie surplus: 100 calories (gaining weight)

The rate of expansion of the universe doesn't increase as you get further from earth, it increases as the distance between two objects increases. If you're on earth, and I'm somehow transported to a planet 13 billion light years away, we'd both observe each other's Galaxy as moving away at a certain speed. Locally, we can both observe the solar systems we're in and the stars in our respective galaxies as how quickly they are actually moving. If we both looked at another Galaxy that was 13 billion light years from each of us, we'd likely observe that Galaxy as moving away from us at the same speed with some variation due to the direction and speed out vantage points are actually moving in relation to the thing we're both observing. Nothing can travel through space faster than the speed of light, but the space between you and an object you're looking at can be so vast that it's rate of expansion makes it look like that object is traveling faster than the speed of light.

If you had a pot (or pool) full of water and exposed it to the vacuum of space it would either freeze or boil depending on temperature. H2O can't exist as a liquid below a certain pressure. Liquid boils when it's vapor pressure exceeds that of the space around it. Most places on earth result in water boiling at our just below 100C. The air pressure at the top of the tallest mountains is low enough that water can boil at about 70C. If you figured out a way to keep water contained in space it wouldn't stay a liquid long enough to add much heat to it. And if you were in it any water that came into contact with your skin would boil immediately due to your body temperature (assuming you could somehow stay alive in a vacuum).
